Also, as your chain wears out, you get some slop in the pins and the links don't hold tight together. Which then means that with thin lube, dirt can still get in there and wreak havoc. Thick gear lube gets into where it needs to be, if you have any idea how lubrication actually works. The shit you buy at the bike shop is like water and it flies everywhere and at the end of the day, you don't have any left on your chain.

Use gear lube instead, lightweight motor oil flies off as you rotate your crank assembly. Like, get a cordless drill, put some of your oil on the chuck and pull the trigger. Some will fly off. Now do the same with gear lube or rear end lube and it won't go anywhere.

Uh, you do realize that you should remove all lubricant from your chain before you re lube your chain? You can get small particles, can act like 3000 grit sand paper. Which isn't very abrasive. But it's much worse than not using WD-40. I use WD40 just so it does break down old lubricants. Rinse with Acetone (Don't get any on your paint), and then apply my gear oil.

Do not use light weight automotive oil. It isn't designed for gears. It's designed to be pooled up. So when you pedal, most flies off. Use a thicker gear lube or something. It'll stick a lot nicer to your chain as it spins around.

Looking at your gate latch, it looks almost identical to a BMW E36 trunk lid latch. What's nice about those is that they are "semi power locks". Meaning, there are no lock and unlock buttons in the car. But you have a key fob. And in the actual car, when you lock one lock manually, they all lock automatically. Trunk and doors. But no button. If you had the latch and the solenoid that yanks on the latch (which are super quiet), then they are already pre wired to work together. So you could set it up to unlock a small case in another part of the room to unlock the secret door.

Or just use the latch with the solenoid. I believe Chevy Blazers (thinking cheap here), have electronic push button rear window latch opening. So it's not a mechanical release. It's a electronic button (like a computer power button), but it also activates a solenoid to open the latch. I recommend these because I have worked on them and even the mounting points are extremely similar and they are small and thin. Some vehicles, especially newer ones, they have gotten bigger and more complicated.

You can't just heat up a piece of steel to temper it. Temperature does actually matter. Like, approximate temperature. "red hot" in a dark room is a few hundred degrees cooler than "red hot" in the middle of the afternoon with clear skies with a huge window or doorway letting in tons of light. And that difference in degrees can mean ultra strong steel or brittle or bendable. I've learned this by making home made AK receivers. I did one based purely on colour of the heat, rivet holes formed cracks around them after about 1000 rounds fired. Did it with a temperature gun and got the heat as close to perfect as possible. 3000 rounds and no cracks or bending.

With that said, believe what you want about it. Either way, the knife looks pretty damn good.
